My wife is always accusing me of cheating and telling me that I'm doing things she finds disrespectful even when I don't mean it like that. For example, she gets offended when I call someone at work "sweetheart." I wish I had a penny for every time she accused me of cheating on her. She doesn't, and never will say she was wrong. How do I get her to understand?

Hello. That must be very frustrating for you to feel that you to be reminded of constant wrongdoing in your relationship, especially when you feel that your wife does not admit to any fault. This could lead you to feel inadequate in the relationship that can harm your relationship in the long-term. Based on what you are reporting and without knowing your wife's side of the story, I would say that you are raising 3 different concerns. One is that there seems to be some concern of infidelity from your wife that you feel is not justified. It may bear clarifying how each of you define "infidelity". Currently, there is no uniform definition of infidelity because it can emcompass a hook-up, chatroom texting, extensive phone calls to a female friend, viewing pornography, a massage with happy ending, physical intercourse, or intimate emotional sharing. Depending on whether any of these circumstances have occured, you may need to reflect whether there is any truth to what she may be accusing you of and for you to share with her your reasons for engaging in these activities. If there is no truth to it, then my clinical intuition is that she may be accusing you of infidelity as a way of saying, "I feel you distancing from me." In other words, it's not so much about whether you are actually unfaithful but a statement of how she feels as she witnesses your distancing from her. Often times, accusing a partner of cheating is likened to a cry or a yearning for closeness. If so, what you want to do is to reflect to her that perhaps she is saying that you are unfaithful because she senses that you are moving away from her emotionally. If this is true, you may wish to share with her why you are pulling away and then discuss the kind of support you may need to feel closer to her again. Otherwise, if the focus becomes about who is right and who is wrong, the conversation will never touch at both of your core emotional needs. The second issue touches upon how to interpret calling someone a "sweetheart." The term has been loosely used in a variety of contexts to mean "you're so sweet and kind", "my dear", or in a flirtatious manner to mean "sweetie." The intention behind the use is known only to the speaker. You may want to reflect in what context you meant to use the term and share it with your wife. If your wife overheard the comment not knowing your intentions or context, it is possible that she may have misinterpreted what you have said.  If she finds the term disrespectful, it may be her way of expressing, "I want to be the important person in your life and if you call someone else a sweetheart it means that I am not valued as much." Therefore, arguing about who has the right or wrong interpretation may be missing the mark. Rather, the issue is about how do you wish to treat or show consideration of each others feelings? You may wish to explore how do you show her that you value her and that she is important to you? Is saying "sweetheart" to another woman conducive to that or is it sending mixed messages to your wife? That said, if you have expressed and shown her that she is important to you on many occasions with open discussions and by understanding, accomodating and prioritizing her needs, then her actions may be a reflection of her personal insecurities. She may need to speak to a therapist about her feelings and her fears.The last issue you raised concerns your wife never admitting she's wrong. Indeed that must be frustrating for you to hear often that you are doing something wrong. In the absence of her admitting to any faults, it could seem like you are the one with the problem. Unfortunately, blaming invites defensiveness and a withdrawn behavior because most people who feel blamed do not feel good about themselves and wishes to distance themselves from the person who is making them feel unhappy. This pattern can also trigger the partners' insecurity as they witnesses the distancing, which could make them angrier and more accusatory - creating a vicious cycle. Finding a healthy way of reaching out when your partner is in turmoil to help calm her emotions and being able to speak about your own feelings and needs is at the heart of a very secure attachment. This kind of conversation can be guided by an experienced professional to help both of you to express your feelings and needs in a safe and secure way to foster a secure bonding. We sometimes take for granted the simple expression of, "I'm sorry." However, it requires a certain comfort with being vulnerable to express that. In my practice, when a client tells me that his or her partner never says "I'm sorry", I am often observing the first partner to see if they are able to express vulnerability. If neither of them express it, then it makes sense to me because why would one risk being vulnerable and then getting hurt if they open up if the other partner doesn't do it.? These insights in therapy can sometimes lead to a different relationship building conversation, which can help couples to to feel safer with each other rather than blaming and alientating. For more information about these services, you are welcome to read my materials on my website at www.PsychologyResource.ca or to contact me at (514) 690-2469.

One approach to managing your anxiety levels in crowded spaces is by gradually exposing yourself to those situations and practicing relaxation techniques. Start by selecting a relatively low-stress environment with few people, such as a small gathering or a quiet park, where you can begin getting accustomed to being around others.

As you become more comfortable in these settings, try gradually increasing the number of people present or moving on to slightly busier locations. This method, known as exposure therapy, can help desensitize you to crowded spaces over time.

In addition to exposure therapy, incorporating relaxation techniques into your daily routine may also be beneficial. Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, and mindfulness meditation are examples of practices that can help reduce anxiety symptoms. You can find guides or videos online that demonstrate these techniques in detail.

Learning to challenge negative thoughts associated with crowded spaces is another helpful strategy. Practice identifying any irrational beliefs or assumptions you might have about being in public places, and work on replacing them with realistic and positive thoughts. For example, instead of thinking "I'm going to have a panic attack if I go to this event," try reframing it as "I may feel anxious, but I can handle it and take steps to manage my anxiety."

Implementing strategies to promote overall well-being can also contribute positively to managing your anxiety. Regular exercise, maintaining a healthy diet, getting enough sleep, and surrounding yourself with supportive individuals can all make a difference. Engaging in activities you enjoy and finding ways to relax and unwind can further aid in reducing stress.

It's worth noting that everyone responds differently to various methods of anxiety management, so what works for one person may not necessarily work for another. If you find that despite your efforts, your symptoms continue to worsen or significantly impact your daily life, seeking professional help from a mental health expert would be advisable.

Remember, managing anxiety is a process, and progress takes time and patience. Celebrate each small milestone along the way, and be kind to yourself as you navigate through this journey of managing your symptoms.

I am a really shy person. I'm currently in a graduate program which requires lots of presentations, but they always make me feel stressed out and less confident. How can I get more confident?

I was the very same way when I was in graduate school.  It makes sense that speaking in front of others would be scary because all of the attention is on you and you probably have expectations to meet each time (including your own).Practice is the best way to build confidence before a speech.  Feeling prepared reduces anxiety for speaking just like it would for taking a test--you are solidifying the pathways in your brain that store and recall the information you need to know and speak about.Remember that it's pretty normal to feel increased anxiety before and during a speech.  It's something that matters to you, so your body is trying to prepare you to fight through it.  It can often feel like your body is working against you when it is actually doing quite the opposite!Also remember that people typically are not aware of how anxious you are.  They cannot hear your heart racing, they don't have access to your racing thoughts or insecurities, and they cannot feel the butterflies in your stomach.  When you practice your speech, practice appearing confident as well.  Identify a couple focal points where you practice and pretend those are people.  Confident posture and eye contact can help you feel more confident about what you are speaking about.  When you get to the actual speech, have a couple focal points that you switch your gaze to every few seconds.  People will perceive that as confidence, even if you aren't looking directly into everyone's eyes (which can be intimidating).Don't forget to breathe!  Taking a few deep breaths can send the message to your brain that what you are about to do is not dangerous--you are safe.  You'll still feel anxiety, but that's OK!  During your presentation, you can continue that in a sense by speaking slower.  It may seem like you are talking too slowly, but when you are anxious, it's actually a natural response to talk too fast.Try to visualize yourself doing well and remind yourself that you can make it through a presentation.  When it's over, give yourself that credit!

I'm currently struggling with diagnosed depression, anxiety, and Misophonia. Also, I am 99% sure I have Borderline Personality Disorder and Avoidant Personality Disorder. I read the DSM-IV, taken college psychology, etc. I know it in my heart I have them. Is self-diagnosing okay with the right research?

Hello, and thank you for your question. Self-diagnosing is something that we all do about one health issue or another. Taking a guess about what may or may not be happening to us is completely normal, however the actual clinical diagnoses of a mental health disorder requires a licensed mental health professional. Here are a few reasons for this: 1. Making a clinical diagnosis often requires other things besides matching up the symptoms of a disorder. To come to a diagnoses for any of the things you mentioned, a counselor would consult the DSM, but they may also use some type of screening tool, assessment or scale. Many disorders have similarities and it requires someone with training to tease out the differences in the symptoms. 2. Our judgement is sometimes off when it comes to assessing ourselves. We really can't be objective. Something as serious as determining a diagnosis really needs to be done by someone who has that objectivity. In addition, once you know your diagnosis, treating it usually requires help from a professional. 3. Sometimes the symptoms of a mental health disorder makes self-diagnoses impossible, in and of itself. For example, someone could be having hallucinations or delusions and not realize it. That would clearly make it impossible for them to diagnose themselves. There a many examples where something like this could happen with different mental health disorders. There are other reasons, but these are three important ones. Now, does this mean that you are wrong about your diagnosis? Maybe not. You may be correct. But, it is important to get this confirmed by a professional mental health clinician. If a disorder is then found, you can begin to talk about treatment. Hope this was helpful. Be well.Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPCC, NCC

I hope through therapy, I can process my feelings and find ways to honor her memory while moving forward.

Losing a loved one can be an incredibly challenging and painful experience, and it's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed with grief and sadness. It's important to allow yourself the time and space to mourn and grieve in your own way.

Crying is a natural response to loss and can be a healthy way to release emotions. Don't try to suppress or ignore those tears. Instead, try to find moments when you can let yourself express whatever comes up for you emotionally. Consider creating a comforting routine or personal ritual that allows you to connect with your feelings and memories of your grandmother.

Guilt is a common emotion that many people experience after losing someone. Remember that no one is perfect, and it's normal to have regrets about not spending as much time as we would have liked with our loved ones. Instead of dwelling on what could have been, focus on cherishing the memories you do have and finding ways to honor her memory.

Therapy can be a valuable tool in helping you process your grief and find ways to honor your grandmother's memory while moving forward. In therapy, you'll have a safe and supportive space to explore your emotions, thoughts, and challenges related to the loss. A therapist can provide guidance and assist you in developing coping strategies tailored to your specific needs.

Consider reaching out to a therapist experienced in grief counseling or even finding support groups where you can share your experiences with others who may be going through similar situations. Talking openly about your feelings with understanding individuals can help validate your emotions and offer comfort.

Additionally, don't underestimate the power of engaging in activities that bring you joy and peace. Honoring your grandmother's memory could involve doing things she enjoyed or carrying on traditions that were meaningful to her. This, along with practicing self-care and seeking support from your loved ones, can aid in the healing process.

Remember that everyone navigates the grieving process at their own pace, so be patient with yourself as you go through ups and downs. Allow yourself to process your grief while also exploring ways to move forward and find meaning in life after loss.
What are symptoms of ‘Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)’?

ADHD symptoms can be divided into three major categories: behavioral, cognitive, and mood. ADHD behavioral symptoms include aggression, excitability, fidgeting, hyperactivity, impulsivity, irritability, and repeated words or actions. Symptoms of cognitive impairment include absentmindedness, difficulty focusing, forgetfulness, attention problems, and short attention spans. There are many mood-related symptoms, such as anger, anxiety, boredom, excitement, and mood swings.

"I've been experiencing intense anxiety recently, especially when I'm in crowded places or social situations. It's getting harder and harder for me to go out and enjoy my daily activities."

Experiencing intense anxiety can be incredibly challenging, but I want you to know that there are steps you can take to manage it. Here are some suggestions that may help:

1. Deep Breathing: When you find yourself in a crowded or social setting and feel your anxiety rising, focus on taking slow, deep breaths. Inhale deeply through your nose, hold the breath for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. This technique can help calm your nervous system.

2. Grounding Techniques: Using grounding techniques can help you stay present and connected to your surroundings. One simple method is to identify five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. Doing this exercise can redirect your attention away from anxious thoughts.

3. Gradual Exposure: Consider gradually exposing yourself to crowded places or social situations with the support of a trusted friend or family member. Start with small steps, such as going to a less crowded place and gradually working your way up to more uncomfortable situations. This exposure therapy technique can help desensitize you to the triggering environment over time.

4. Self-Care Routine: Prioritizing self-care activities can greatly contribute to managing anxiety. Make sure to engage in activities that bring you joy and relaxation, such as reading, practicing mindfulness, engaging in hobbies, or spending time in nature. Taking care of your physical health by exercising regularly, eating nutritious meals, and getting adequate sleep can also have positive effects on your overall well-being.

5. Cognitive-Behavioral Techniques: Challenging negative thoughts associated with social situations can be helpful. Notice when you have anxious thoughts and try to replace them with more realistic and positive ones. Remind yourself that you are capable of handling these situations and that anxiety does not define you.

6. Seek Support: Reach out to supportive friends or family members who can offer understanding and encouragement during this challenging time. Sometimes talking to someone who has experienced similar anxiety can provide valuable insights and coping strategies.

Remember, managing anxiety takes time and patience. Don't be too hard on yourself if progress feels slow at times. With consistent effort and employing various techniques, you may find that your anxiety gradually lessens, enabling you to enjoy your daily activities once again.

A girl and I were madly in love. We dated for over a year and were even talking about marriage and future plans together. She moved away for school, and we attempted a long distance relationship. We eventually broke up. It's been a year now, and I still haven't lost my feelings for her. I still love her the same way I did. I've suffered from depression ever since the breakup and have been unable to connect with anyone else. It's damaging me and my life.

Hi Boise, I'm sorry that you've lost this love. The fact that you were planning marriage and a future tells me that you meant something very special to each other at that time. It's different now...you're not together anymore, but you can't accept this, right? Good for you for identifying that this situation is damaging your life. You've been grieving for longer than you were together. Oh, but really you've not been grieving...you're stuck still loving her instead of moving forward. Unrequited love is a recipe for eternal heartache. Let's look at some possible blocks to moving forward.It could be that there's something unfinished for you. Maybe you felt hurt and you didn't have the chance to say so, or you felt you hurt her and you didn't have the chance to make it right. Maybe there's a burning question you need to ask or something else you need to say. Maybe you want to tell her you've never stopped loving her, and see if she feels the same way. If this is the case, you have two choices, right? You can reach out and say what you need to say, or you can stop ruminating on that question and let it go. If you reach out, there's no guarantee it will go well or that she'll even respond. Maybe write her a letter and don't send it (or send it...it might be worth the risk). Use the next paragraph to help you decide. Do you know how she feels? How did it end? Did she end it? Was it ended just because of the distance, or are there more differences between you that didn't work? Sometimes people are so in love that they can't clearly see that the other person isn't in love with them anymore. Use the information you have about what she wants for her life...can you honour what she says she needs? If she's asked for distance, you would do well to honour that.A key to moving forward: look at your thoughts and where they're getting stuck. Write it down. What bad thing can happen if you let it go? Or "If I move forward, that will mean..."  Keep going...what would be the worst part of that?  This kind of exploring can help you identify your stuck place.It is possible that you've turned this ending into some kind of negative meaning about you or your future. As in "If this person doesn't love me, then I'm unlovable", or "No one will ever love me as much as she did". So your need to cling to her in your heart is your way of rejecting that negative message about yourself or the future. Can you find another way to reject that message? Try saying these things to yourself:I know she loved me. There is evidence of that.I was a good partner. There is evidence of that.It's part of life to fall in love and then have to move forward...I can do this and learn from it.Many people like me...that's how I know I'm lovable.It's normal to feel sad. I'm grieving a lost love.I want to move forward and not stare in the rearview mirror.I know more love awaits me if I can get fear out of the way.If this person loved me, others can too, (but not if I'm clinging to some old memory)These are the kinds of things a therapist would explore with you. I wish you well!

In my friendships, I often find myself being the one who puts in more effort and gives more support than I receive in return. It leaves me feeling drained and unappreciated. I value these connections, but sometimes it feels like they're one-sided. How can I establish healthier boundaries and ensure that my friendships are mutually supportive?

It can be really tough when you feel like you're putting in more effort and support into your friendships than you receive in return. It's completely understandable that this leaves you feeling drained and unappreciated. Building healthier boundaries and creating mutually supportive friendships is definitely possible, so let's explore some suggestions together.

Firstly, it might be helpful to reflect on what you need from your friendships and what your expectations are. Understanding your own needs will allow you to communicate them effectively with your friends. Consider the kind of support you would like to receive and how often. This self-awareness will help guide you in establishing healthier boundaries.

Once you have a clear understanding of your needs, try expressing them openly and honestly with your friends. Communication is key in any relationship. Let them know how important their support is to you and how you'd appreciate a more balanced give-and-take dynamic. Remember, your friends may not even realize that they're not meeting your expectations unless you express it to them.

Additionally, setting boundaries is crucial for maintaining healthy relationships. Identify where you feel comfortable drawing the line and communicate those boundaries kindly but firmly. For example, if you find yourself constantly being available for others at the expense of your own well-being, it could be beneficial to establish specific times or days dedicated solely to self-care.

Remember that it's okay to prioritize your own needs and take care of yourself. Sometimes, we unintentionally attract people who rely heavily on us without reciprocating the same level of support. By focusing on building relationships with individuals who value and respect your efforts, you can create a more balanced and fulfilling social circle.

Lastly, don't hesitate to seek out new connections as well. Expanding your social network can introduce you to people who naturally align with your values and provide the mutual support you desire. Joining clubs, organizations, or engaging in activities that interest you can be great ways to meet like-minded individuals.

I hope these suggestions help you establish healthier boundaries and cultivate more mutually supportive friendships. Remember, it's important to surround yourself with people who appreciate and value your efforts. You deserve to have relationships that uplift and energize you.

"I feel distant from my partner and I want to work on our intimacy."
 Lately, I've noticed a growing distance between my partner and me. We used to have such a strong connection, but now it feels like we're living separate lives. I miss the intimacy we once had. I hope through counseling, we can explore the underlying issues and rebuild that emotional and physical closeness.

Building and maintaining intimacy in a relationship is important for emotional and physical closeness. It's great that you recognize the growing distance between you and your partner and want to work on it. Here are some suggestions to help you rebuild intimacy:

1. Open communication: Start by having an open and honest conversation with your partner about how you've been feeling. Express your concerns, desires, and hopes for rebuilding the connection. Encourage your partner to share their thoughts and feelings as well. Active listening can foster understanding and bring you closer together.

2. Quality time: Set aside dedicated time to spend with each other without distractions. Engage in activities that you both enjoy or try new ones together. This can help create shared experiences and strengthen your bond. Make sure to prioritize this time consistently to nurture the intimacy.

3. Emotional support: Show empathy and support for your partner's emotions and challenges. Validate their feelings and be there for them during difficult times. Offering comfort and reassurance helps build trust and deepens emotional intimacy.

4. Physical touch: Physical affection plays a crucial role in building and maintaining intimacy. Small gestures like holding hands, hugging, and kissing can contribute to a sense of closeness. Initiate physical contact and express your love and attraction towards your partner through gentle touches.

5. Explore interests together: Find common interests or hobbies that you can engage in as a couple. This could range from going for walks or cooking together to joining classes or pursuing shared passions. Having shared activities fosters a sense of unity and encourages bonding.

6. Prioritize self-care: Take care of yourself individually, as it impacts the overall health of your relationship. Nurture your own mental and emotional well-being, engage in activities that make you happy, and maintain a healthy work-life balance. When you feel fulfilled personally, it can positively influence your connection with your partner.

7. Seek professional help if needed: While these suggestions can be helpful, sometimes professional guidance can provide additional support. If you find that your efforts alone don't yield the desired results, consider seeking couples therapy or relationship counseling. A trained professional can assist in understanding underlying issues and provide effective strategies for rebuilding intimacy.

Remember, rebuilding intimacy takes time, effort, and commitment from both partners. Be patient with each other as you navigate this process together. By being open, supportive, and willing to invest in your relationship, you have a higher chance of reconnecting emotionally and physically.

I just took a job that requires me to travel far away from home. My family and I really need this job.
   People keep telling me I have "anxiety" and I'm terrified of having an anxiety attack on the road. This is all new to me. What can I do?

First of all, congratulations on your new role! Transitions can be challenging, and it sounds like you are experiencing a lot of change.  This would be difficult for many people, and it seems that you have an added layer of challenge.  I recommend visiting a therapist to determine the root cause of your anxiety and working to unravel those causes piece by piece. I know seeing a therapist can be challenging when traveling, and online counseling could be a good solution. In the meantime, here are a few of my favorite anxiety stopping strategies.  1. Grounding Exercises: When you feel your anxiety increasing, take a deep breath and begin things in your room (or where ever you are) that have things in common. For example, name all of the blue things that you can see.  You can also do non-visual grounding exercises like naming all of the hte sports teams you can think of or all of the state capitals.  This will get your mind off of your anxiety and connect you to space.  2. The pretzel: This is a seated pose that will stop any anxiety attack in its tracks.  Start in a seated position and cross your dominate leg over your nondominant leg. Then, stretch your arms out in front of you with the back of your hands facing one another.  Cross your arms in front of each other so that your palms are touching.  Flip your arms into your body.  You will end with your elbows by your side and your hands crossed under your chin.  Close your eyes and take long breaths in through your nose and out through your mouth.  This calming pose will help you get through even the toughest of panic episodes. 3. Bilateral stimulation and visualization: Start in a seated position with your hands placed on your knees. Tap each knee in an alternating pattern. Close your eyes and begin visualizing a peaceful setting. The combination of bilateral stimulation and visualization will help calm your body and mind.  I could go on and on, but these techniques should get you started.  These techniques should help you manage anxiety in a pinch.  Best of luck!

How does a person start the counseling process?

A great place to start is at www.psychologytoday.com.  You can search by location and identify therapists who have expertise in your area of concern.  Once you find a few people that fit your criteria, read about them on Psychology today as well as check out their website if they have one.  Next, either call or email them to set up a time to talk for a few minutes.  When you speak with them, you want to know a few things: do they have a decent amount of experience in your area of concern?  Are their fees, insurance coverage and scheduling availability a good fit for you?  Most importantly, see if you feel comfortable when you speak to them on the phone!  If this person is a good match in these areas, schedule an initial consultation so that you can see if you are also a good match in person.

Hello, and thank you for your question. First, I want to tell you how sorry I am for the experience you had with your parents. That is a grief and trauma that is certainly hard to imagine. Trauma and grief can affect us in many ways, and certainly deeply personal things like our sex lives. It may be difficult for others to make the connection, but it is there. If your husband will agree to it, couple's counseling may be your best bet. If he doesn't agree to go, it may be worth it to go on your own. You still have a lot you are dealing with yourself. And sometimes our personally therapy can influence others, so it may be a good idea. It is important to remember that even though you are married you have the right to make decisions about your body, and that includes when you want to have sex with it. Personal flaws: Some emperors were simply bad rulers due to personal flaws such as greed, cruelty, or incompetence.
External pressures: The Roman Empire faced a number of external pressures, including economic crises, military threats, and natural disasters. These challenges often put pressure on emperors to make unpopular decisions or take drastic measures that could harm their reputation.

The thought of everyone's attention being on me made me feel incredibly anxious. The symptoms of anxiety that I experience include racing thoughts, restlessness, muscle tension, a sense of impending doom, and difficulty sleeping. These symptoms happen multiple times a week and can last for hours each time.

To manage your anxiety better and reduce its impact on your life, there are several strategies you can try. It's important to note that while I can offer some general guidance, it may be beneficial to consult with a mental health professional who can provide personalized support.

1. Deep Breathing Exercises: When you feel overwhelmed or anxious, deep breathing exercises can help calm your body and mind. Take slow, deep breaths in through your nose, hold for a few seconds, and exhale slowly through your mouth. Repeat this process for a few minutes, focusing solely on your breath.

2. Progressive Muscle Relaxation: This technique involves tensing and then releasing each muscle group in your body to promote relaxation. Start by tensing the muscles in your toes, gradually working your way up to your head. Hold the tension for a few seconds, then release and notice the difference in sensations between tension and relaxation.

 
3. Challenge Negative Thoughts: Anxiety often stems from negative thoughts or worries about potential outcomes. Take time to identify any recurring negative thoughts related to situations where you feel overwhelmed or out of control. Once identified, question the evidence supporting these thoughts and consider alternative perspectives that might be more realistic and positive.

4. Grounding Techniques: If you find yourself caught up in racing thoughts or feelings of impending doom, grounding techniques can help bring your focus back to the present moment. Try engaging your senses by focusing on what you can see, hear, smell, taste, and touch in your immediate surroundings.

5. Prioritize Self-Care: Taking care of yourself physically, mentally, and emotionally is essential when managing anxiety. Ensure you're getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, and engaging in regular physical activity. Additionally, practicing stress-reducing activities such as mindfulness meditation, yoga, or spending time in nature can also have a positive impact.

6. Gradual Exposure: Consider gradually exposing yourself to situations that trigger your anxiety, starting with less overwhelming scenarios and gradually working your way up. This exposure allows you to build resilience and confidence over time.

Remember, these are general suggestions that may not apply in all situations. It can be helpful to assess which strategies work best for you personally. As a mental health professional, ensuring the confidentiality of our conversations is an essential part of the therapeutic process. Your trust in maintaining this confidentiality is crucial for creating a safe and secure environment.

One important aspect to consider is that therapists have a legal and ethical obligation to maintain client confidentiality. This means that anything you share during our sessions should remain private unless there are specific circumstances where your safety or someone else's safety may be at risk.

To address your concerns further, it can be helpful to discuss the specific rules and regulations regarding confidentiality with your therapist. They will likely provide you with detailed information on how they handle confidentiality, such as what might be disclosed without your consent and under what circumstances.

Therapists often follow certain guidelines when sharing information. For example, they may consult with other professionals (without identifying you) to seek guidance on best practices, but any details that could identify you would be carefully withheld.

It’s also worth noting that the therapeutic space itself aims to create a confidential environment by taking specific measures. These measures include having private consultation rooms, using secure electronic systems to store your information, and ensuring that unauthorized individuals do not have access to the data.

If you still have concerns about the security of your information, I encourage you to openly discuss them with your therapist. This way, you both can collaboratively find ways to address those concerns and establish that strong foundation of trust so vital for therapy to progress effectively.

Remember, building a healthy therapeutic relationship involves open communication, so don't hesitate to voice any reservations or questions you have regarding confidentiality.

There are specific therapies that have shown effectiveness in treating trauma, such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR).

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy focuses on identifying and challenging negative thought patterns and beliefs associated with the traumatic event. Through CBT, you can learn coping skills, relaxation techniques, and strategies to gradually face situations or triggers that provoke fear and anxiety. Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing utilizes bilateral stimulation, typically eye movements, to process and integrate traumatic memories in a new and less distressing way. The recent loss of a loved one has triggered a deep sadness within me that I can't seem to shake off. It's impacting my ability to function normally and engage in day-to-day activities. Today, I hope to explore ways to navigate the grieving process and find comfort during this challenging time.

Losing a loved one can be an incredibly difficult and painful experience, and it's understandable that you're feeling deep sadness right now. Grief is a complex journey that affects everyone differently, but there are some strategies that may help you navigate through this challenging time.

First, it might be helpful to create space for your emotions and allow yourself to grieve. This means giving yourself permission to feel sad, angry, or whatever other feelings arise. Sometimes we try to push these feelings away, but acknowledging them can ultimately lead to healing.

Additionally, finding healthy outlets for your emotions could provide comfort and relief. Engaging in activities that bring you joy or solace, such as spending time with supportive friends or family, taking walks in nature, engaging in hobbies, or practicing mindfulness or meditation, can help you process your emotions while also providing moments of respite.

Grieving also involves adjusting to a new reality without your loved one. It may be helpful to establish a routine that gives your days structure and provides a sense of stability during this uncertain time. Setting small goals for each day, even if they seem insignificant, can give you a sense of purpose and accomplishment.

Seeking support from others who have experienced loss can also be beneficial. Connecting with support groups or online communities where people share similar experiences allows for validation, empathy, and understanding. Surrounding yourself with individuals who have gone through similar circumstances can provide comfort and guidance as you move through the grieving process.

Lastly, it's important to prioritize self-care. Taking care of your physical and emotional needs can contribute to your overall well-being during this time of grief. Make sure to eat balanced meals, exercise regularly, get enough sleep, and engage in activities that nourish your soul.

Remember that grief takes time and everyone's process is unique. Be patient with yourself as you navigate through this journey. If you find that your symptoms worsen or persist over time, consider reaching out to a mental health professional for additional support.

I hope these suggestions provide some guidance as you navigate the grieving process. Remember that healing is possible, and even though it may seem difficult now, with time and support, you will find comfort in the memories you shared with your loved one while also creating new ones moving forward.

What is the best watch in the world ?

No one watch qualifies as best. It depends on an individual's preferences. Broadly watches can be classified into Digital and Mechanical watches. Mechanical watches can be further categorized into automatic and non-automatic. 

Digital watches typically use an electronic circuit to keep track of time. They generally are mass-produced and are inexpensive but highly accurate in keeping time. 

On the other hand, Mechanical Automatic watches typically use a rotor, or metal weight, to power the timepiece and keep time. The rotor is powered by the movement of the watch wearer's hand. Premium watches are handmade and can be pretty expensive. They also are the least accurate in keeping time. However, watch enthusiasts still love and collect these watches. 

Mechanical non-automatic watches typically use a quartz crystal to keep track of time. These are inexpensive and very accurate at keeping time. 

So the best watch for you depends on what you are looking for. If you have a tight budget and care about accurate timing, then digital or non-automatic watches might work well. On the other hand, if you are a watch enthusiast, then Automatic watches are a great buy.

Your struggle is understandable, and it's important to remember that emotions are a natural part of being human. The ADAPT model, which stands for Acknowledge, Define, Adjust, and Practice, can be a helpful framework for managing emotions and impulsive actions. Let's start by acknowledging your emotions and impulses. This means accepting that they are a part of you and recognizing that they are valid. It's essential to understand that emotions are not good or bad, they just are. Now, let's move on to defining the problem. This involves identifying the specific emotions and triggers that are causing your impulsive actions. We can use a problem checklist to help us with this. This checklist includes identifying the problem, understanding the problem, determining the cause of the problem, and setting specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART) goals.

For example, if your emotional rollercoaster is often triggered by feelings of sadness or loneliness, we can explore the underlying causes of these emotions. Perhaps there's a specific relationship or situation that's causing you to feel this way. Or maybe there's a deeper emotional wound that's being reopened. By gaining a clearer understanding of the underlying causes of your emotions, we can begin to address them in a healthy and productive way.

Additionally, it's important to recognize that emotions are complex and multifaceted. They can be influenced by a variety of factors, including biological, psychological, and environmental factors. For instance, hormonal imbalances, trauma, or stress can all contribute to intense emotions and impulsive actions. By taking a holistic approach to understanding your emotions, we can develop a more comprehensive and effective approach to managing them.

Once we've identified the underlying causes of your emotions and triggers, we can begin to adjust your thoughts and behaviors to better manage them. This might involve learning new coping skills, such as mindfulness meditation or cognitive restructuring. It could also involve making lifestyle changes, such as getting regular exercise or improving your diet. By taking a proactive and compassionate approach to managing your emotions, you can begin to break free from the cycle of impulsive actions and develop a greater sense of emotional resilience.

I encourage you to practice this exercise regularly, as it can help you develop a deeper understanding of your emotions and triggers, and ultimately, lead to healthier and more productive ways of coping with them. Since then, I have been struggling to find joy in activities that used to bring me happiness, such as spending time with friends or pursuing hobbies. These symptoms of depression occur almost every day and persist over several weeks. They are accompanied by physical manifestations like changes in appetite, difficulty concentrating, and constant fatigue.

Reflecting on my past experiences, there have been instances of childhood trauma that may contribute to my current challenges. Growing up, I faced emotional neglect due to a lack of parental support. This has made it difficult for me to form healthy relationships and trust others. Coping with depression, I have tried engaging in mindfulness practices like meditation, which temporarily alleviate some of my distress. However, I am eager to explore additional coping mechanisms or therapy options that could provide more lasting relief.

During our session, I would appreciate discussing different treatment approaches for depression. In particular, I am curious about the effectiveness of medication in conjunction with talk therapy. It sounds like you've been going through a difficult time lately, and it's understandable that you're feeling overwhelmed by sadness and hopelessness. The fact that you want to understand your depression better and develop strategies for improving your mental well-being is an important step towards healing.

The breakup of a long-term relationship can indeed be a significant trigger for feelings of abandonment and questioning self-worth. It's common to struggle with finding joy in activities that used to bring happiness during periods of depression. The physical manifestations you mentioned, such as changes in appetite, difficulty concentrating, and constant fatigue, are also common symptoms experienced by many individuals dealing with depression.

Considering your childhood experiences of emotional neglect, it's possible that these past traumas may contribute to the challenges you face now. Difficulty forming healthy relationships and trusting others is a common consequence of such experiences. Engaging in mindfulness practices like meditation is great for temporarily alleviating distress, but it's natural to seek additional coping mechanisms or therapy options for more lasting relief.

In terms of treatment approaches for depression, there are various options available. Medication can be effective for some people, especially when used in conjunction with talk therapy. Some medications help regulate mood and manage symptoms, while therapy provides a space to address underlying issues and develop coping skills. Therapy can also help in navigating the stigma associated with mental health issues and incorporating self-care practices into your daily routine.

Remember that everyone's journey with depression is unique, and what works for one person might not work for another. It's essential to find a treatment plan tailored to your specific needs and preferences. It could be beneficial to explore different therapy modalities, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy, dialectical behavior therapy, or psychodynamic therapy, to see which approach resonates with you.

Regarding stigma, it can be challenging when society views mental health issues differently from physical health issues. However, more and more people are speaking up about mental health, which helps break down the barriers of stigma. Surrounding yourself with supportive friends and family who understand or educating others about mental health can be steps towards combating this stigma. Incorporating self-care practices into your daily routine, such as maintaining a healthy lifestyle, engaging in activities you enjoy, and prioritizing self-compassion, can also contribute to your overall well-being.

Remember, breaking free from depression takes time and effort. Be patient with yourself, celebrate small victories, and reach out for support when needed. I'm here to help guide you through this process and provide additional resources if necessary.

There is no scientifically established formula for understanding dreams, that I know about, however, many people get a great deal of value from exploring what their dreams mean. It is believed by many that our dreams contain metaphors that represent meaningful patterns in our lives and relationships and if we pay attention to them we can learn important things about ourselves. One thing you might try, to see if you can get more insight into the dream and possibly begin remembering things, is to take note of whatever you do remember, any details about your experience, such as when do you wake up from the dream, how do you feel, both emotionally and physically, what are you thinking about when you wake up, is there any pattern in terms of what happens to you in your waking life around the time you have this dream... If you can keep a journal or a recording device to speak into by your bed, you can try to record whatever you do remember and notice as soon as you wake up. People seem to have more difficulty remembering dreams, the more time they let go by before attempting to record the dream, or if you go back to sleep before recording what you remember.

My goal today is to address my anxiety and find ways to minimize its impact on my daily life. Over the past few weeks, I've been experiencing ongoing restlessness and worry about various aspects of my personal and professional life. These feelings of unease often escalate into panic episodes, during which I struggle to control my racing thoughts and physical symptoms such as sweating and trembling. Last Monday, I had to deliver an important presentation at work, which triggered severe anxiety. Despite thorough preparation, I was plagued by self-doubt, resulting in impaired concentration and shaky voice during the presentation. It has become increasingly challenging for me to handle these anxious moments and continue functioning optimally.

To address your anxiety and minimize its impact on your daily life, there are several strategies you can try:

1. Deep Breathing: When you feel anxious or have a panic episode, focus on taking slow, deep breaths. Inhale deeply through your nose, hold the breath for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. This technique helps activate your body's relaxation response and can help reduce physical symptoms such as sweating and trembling.

2. Grounding Techniques: During moments of anxiety, it may be helpful to ground yourself in the present moment by using your senses. For example, you can name five things you see around you, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. This exercise helps redirect your focus away from racing thoughts and brings your attention back to the present.

3. Cognitive Restructuring: Challenge negative and self-doubting thoughts that contribute to your anxiety. Ask yourself if there is evidence to support these thoughts or if they are based on assumptions. Then, try to reframe them with more realistic and positive alternatives. For instance, instead of thinking "I always mess up presentations," you could replace it with "I have successfully delivered presentations in the past, and I can do it again."

4. Self-Care: Make sure you are prioritizing self-care activities that promote relaxation and well-being. Engage in activities that bring you joy and help you unwind, such as exercising regularly, practicing mindfulness or meditation, pursuing hobbies, spending time in nature, or connecting with loved ones. Taking care of your physical and emotional health can enhance your overall resilience towards anxiety.

5. Seek Support: It can be beneficial to talk about your feelings with someone you trust, like a friend or family member. Sharing your experiences with others who may have similar struggles can provide validation and support. Additionally, consider seeking professional help if your anxiety continues to significantly impact your daily functioning. A mental health professional can provide you with personalized guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

Remember, managing anxiety is a process, and it may take time to find what techniques work best for you. Be patient with yourself as you explore different strategies, and celebrate small victories along the way.

It sounds like you are noticing that you are drawn towards sad and negative content and it's hard to understand why. This may sound counter-intuitive, but sometimes we do things that on the surface may look problematic (or even cause us some real problems) because it serves us in some unseen way. A simple example would be somebody who is addicted to a substance; their addiction may be causing serious problems in their life, and they may even know it, but the addiction serves them by helping them to avoid painful feelings that they anticipate having if they quit using. Now I am not saying that what you describe is an addiction, it is just a really illustrative example of the unseen benefit.One thing I would be wondering about is what is the unseen benefit of seeking out sad and negative content? I'd also be wondering what your relationship is to other feelings. These are things you may benefit from exploring with a competent therapist.

I'm a teenager, and I just got my first job. I am a month and a half in. Yesterday, my boss pushed me to the point where I had to go to the restroom and cry. She didn't see me, and I'm glad, but when I went to talk to her about it today, I let a tear or two come out. I hate it. I feel like they're not going to keep me anymore.

Getting your first job is an exciting, terrifying, and challenging experience. It is something you will remember for a long time and it shapes how you begin to think about yourself as a worker. You are literally "learning as you go" in this completely new environment. You are going to make mistakes. You are not going to get it right the first time. It can be even more challenging if you are having a difficult time building relationships that are supportive at work. A couple of things to remember here: 1) You are there to do a job and you are getting paid to do it, 2) There is a reason or reasons for you wanting to be there and do that work, 3) you know best what you need in order to be successful. These three items can be helpful to remember, especially when we feel our emotions are taking over in a place where we do not feel safe to express them fully. If you feel like your supervisor is approachable, meaning someone you could talk to because they express confidence in you, let them know you are nervous about doing a good job. Also let them know how you learn new tasks, information, or expectations so they can deliver the message in a way that you understand. Becoming a successful worker doesn't happen overnight, but each day you can identify what works for you and what doesn't by communicating with your work team, the easier it will be for you. We all had a first job once, and were all worried about doing well. Hang in there, and call a counselor if you need more help.

Interacting in social settings overwhelms me to the point where I avoid them altogether. I'd like support in navigating social situations with more confidence.

 My goal is to develop strategies that enable me to engage comfortably in social settings and overcome my social anxiety.

Description of emotions and thoughts, possible triggers: Social events filled with unfamiliar faces trigger a deep sense of insecurity and self-doubt. Thoughts like "What if I say something wrong?" or "They won't like me" flood my mind before and during social interactions.

Specific examples of triggering situations: Last month, I attended a work conference where networking was needed. Seeing everyone mingling effortlessly only heightened my feelings of inadequacy. Eventually, I secluded myself in the corner, unable to engage.

Symptoms: In social situations, my heart races, palms sweat, and my voice tends to tremble. These physical symptoms often persist throughout the event but subside shortly after it ends.

Relevant life events: Experiences of bullying during high school left long-lasting scars and might be linked to my current struggles with social anxiety.

Coping strategies: Currently, I try taking slow breaths and reminding myself that others likely feel similarly anxious. However, these methods don't ease my discomfort significantly enough to confidently interact socially.

Questions/Inquiries: How can therapy help me overcome social anxiety? Are there specific techniques you recommend for managing anxiety in social situations?

Navigating social situations can be challenging, but it's great that you're seeking support to overcome your social anxiety and develop strategies for more comfortable engagement. Therapy can indeed assist you in achieving your goal. Here are some techniques that may help you manage anxiety in social settings:

1. Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT): CBT can be effective in addressing the negative thoughts and self-doubt that arise before and during social interactions. A therapist trained in CBT can work with you to identify and challenge these unhelpful thoughts, replacing them with more realistic and positive ones.

2. Exposure Therapy: This technique involves gradually exposing yourself to feared social situations while practicing relaxation techniques or coping skills. By repeatedly facing these situations, you can desensitize yourself to the anxiety they provoke, allowing you to engage more comfortably over time.

3. Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction: Practicing mindfulness can enhance your ability to stay present in social interactions instead of getting caught up in anxious thoughts. Focusing on your breath or grounding yourself in the current moment can reduce anxiety symptoms and improve overall well-being.

4. Social Skills Training: Engaging in therapy sessions focused on developing social skills can be beneficial. Your therapist can provide guidance and support as you practice assertiveness, active listening, and other essential communication skills. Role-playing exercises may also help build confidence in various social scenarios.

5. Identifying Triggers and Coping Strategies: Reflect on specific situations that trigger your social anxiety. Knowing your triggers allows you to prepare for them. Talk to your therapist about implementing personalized coping strategies such as deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or visualization techniques.

6. Understanding Past Experiences: It's important to address any past experiences, like bullying, that have contributed to your current struggles. Your therapist can help you process these events, challenge distorted beliefs related to them, and cultivate a more positive self-image.

Remember, progress takes time, and everyone's journey is unique. Be patient with yourself as you work through these strategies and seek support from friends or loved ones. By seeking therapy and implementing these techniques, you can build confidence and find greater ease in social interactions.

A girl and I were madly in love. We dated for over a year and were even talking about marriage and future plans together. She moved away for school, and we attempted a long distance relationship. We eventually broke up. It's been a year now, and I still haven't lost my feelings for her. I still love her the same way I did. I've suffered from depression ever since the breakup and have been unable to connect with anyone else. It's damaging me and my life.

Hi Boise, I'm sorry that you've lost this love. The fact that you were planning marriage and a future tells me that you meant something very special to each other at that time. It's different now...you're not together anymore, but you can't accept this, right? Good for you for identifying that this situation is damaging your life. You've been grieving for longer than you were together. Oh, but really you've not been grieving...you're stuck still loving her instead of moving forward. Unrequited love is a recipe for eternal heartache. Let's look at some possible blocks to moving forward.It could be that there's something unfinished for you. Maybe you felt hurt and you didn't have the chance to say so, or you felt you hurt her and you didn't have the chance to make it right. Maybe there's a burning question you need to ask or something else you need to say. Maybe you want to tell her you've never stopped loving her, and see if she feels the same way. If this is the case, you have two choices, right? You can reach out and say what you need to say, or you can stop ruminating on that question and let it go. If you reach out, there's no guarantee it will go well or that she'll even respond. Maybe write her a letter and don't send it (or send it...it might be worth the risk). Use the next paragraph to help you decide. Do you know how she feels? How did it end? Did she end it? Was it ended just because of the distance, or are there more differences between you that didn't work? Sometimes people are so in love that they can't clearly see that the other person isn't in love with them anymore. Use the information you have about what she wants for her life...can you honour what she says she needs? If she's asked for distance, you would do well to honour that.A key to moving forward: look at your thoughts and where they're getting stuck. Write it down. What bad thing can happen if you let it go? Or "If I move forward, that will mean..."  Keep going...what would be the worst part of that?  This kind of exploring can help you identify your stuck place.It is possible that you've turned this ending into some kind of negative meaning about you or your future. As in "If this person doesn't love me, then I'm unlovable", or "No one will ever love me as much as she did". So your need to cling to her in your heart is your way of rejecting that negative message about yourself or the future. Can you find another way to reject that message? Try saying these things to yourself:I know she loved me. There is evidence of that.I was a good partner. There is evidence of that.It's part of life to fall in love and then have to move forward...I can do this and learn from it.Many people like me...that's how I know I'm lovable.It's normal to feel sad. I'm grieving a lost love.I want to move forward and not stare in the rearview mirror.I know more love awaits me if I can get fear out of the way.If this person loved me, others can too, (but not if I'm clinging to some old memory)These are the kinds of things a therapist would explore with you. I wish you well!

A long long time ago the Queen of Odisha heard that there was a master stone sculptor who made such stunning statues of the gods that people would weep from happiness at the beauty of the statues if they saw them. One summer day, while resting indolently with the King in the main hall of the royal palace, the Queen suddenly had a thought. "How nice it would be, King, if we could build some beautiful statutes of Lord Jagannath so that the people can come worship Jagannath, Balabhadra, and Subadhra. What do you think?" 

The King thought for a few minutes, and then nodded in agreement. "What do you have in mind, my Queen?" And so, soon the stone sculptor was summoned to appear before the Court for an appointment to build in his way the statutes of the gods. Soon the monsoon season started and the sculptor appeared in front of the court, awaiting his appointment. He was a humble man from the mountainous regions of Odisha. Even at his best-dressed, one couldn't help but notice his rough hands, and the small sprinkling of dust that seemed ever present in his hair. 

The King and Queen graciously waited as the sculptor bowed and then asked "Your majesties, what can I do for you?" The Queen leaned forward in her throne and her voice rang out in the court "We have heard, o Master Sculptor, of your skills from people far and wide across the Kingdom. We dream of having you put your skills to use to build beautiful statues that will represent Lord Jagannath, Subhadra, and Balabhadra for our people to worship."

The sculptor was silent. As his silence extended, ministers of the court began to feel restless. "Speak up! How can you be silent when the Queen graces you so!" But still, the sculptor was silent. 

The King and Queen sat patiently in their thrones as they waited for the sculptor to respond. Perhaps the enormity of the task was too much. Perhaps, the sculptor was thinking of what he should ask for in return. Or even more, perhaps, the sculptor was awed and honored by the request. 

At last, as the shadows from the late afternoon sun began to stretch across the floors of the hall, the sculptor shifted his weight, and opened his mouth to speak. "Your majesties, you grace me with such a request, I cannot help but oblige. It is an honor." At this, the Queen sat as straight as a rod, listening for the words that would come next. "But, I can do this on one condition only. I will work in a closed hall, where none may enter - regardless of whether they can hear me working or otherwise. None may enter until I open the doors from within and proclaim to all that the statues are completed."

The ministers gasped - what a strange request from this man. Was he a fool? What if he just slept and ate and didn't do any work? How could the King and Queen trust that he would do the work he was promising to do? The Queen looked on thoughtfully. She glanced at the King, and it seemed to her that he agreed on this condition without reservation. She looked at the sculptor and then nodded her assent. "We decree that you shall build these statues in a hall set aside, into which no one shall enter until your work is complete and you proclaim that to us after opening the doors of the hall from within."

Description of emotions/thoughts: Lately, I find myself grappling with ethical dilemmas at work that leave me confused, stressed, and questioning the integrity of certain practices.

Specific triggering event: During a recent team meeting, we were tasked with implementing cost-cutting measures that compromised patient safety. The dilemma forced me to contemplate the balance between organizational demands and my moral obligations.

Symptoms: Ethical conflicts lead to increased anxiety levels and difficulty concentrating on my work tasks. These conflicts preoccupy my thoughts and impact my overall job satisfaction.

Relevant life events: Throughout my childhood, my parents instilled strong moral values within our family. Witnessing their commitment to these principles has shaped my understanding of ethics, making it challenging to compromise them.

Coping strategies: In times of ethical distress, I seek support from trusted colleagues to validate my feelings and gain insight into different perspectives. Reflecting upon ethical guidelines and consulting relevant literature also helps guide my decision-making process.

Question for therapist: How can I navigate ethical dilemmas in a professional setting while maintaining personal and professional integrity? Do you have any advice on effectively communicating my concerns to superiors?

In navigating ethical dilemmas in a professional setting while maintaining personal and professional integrity, there are several steps you can take:

1. Clarify your values: Start by examining your own values and ethics. Reflect on what is truly important to you in terms of patient care, safety, and ethical conduct. This will serve as a compass for making difficult decisions when faced with conflicting situations.

2. Educate yourself: Stay up-to-date with professional guidelines, codes of conduct, and laws relevant to your field. Familiarize yourself with the ethical principles that should guide decision-making in your profession. This knowledge will help you articulate your concerns and provide a framework for discussions with superiors.

3. Assess the situation: Consider the specific context and circumstances surrounding the ethical dilemma. Evaluate the potential risks and consequences associated with different actions or non-actions. Assess the impact on patient safety, organizational reputation, and your own well-being.

4. Seek support: Engage in open dialogue with trusted colleagues who share similar values. Discussing your concerns and gaining their insights can be helpful. Remember to maintain confidentiality and seek advice discreetly without breaching any professional boundaries.

5. Communicate assertively: When addressing ethical concerns with superiors, it is important to approach the conversation diplomatically but assertively. Prepare clear and concise statements about the ethical conflict, its implications, and alternatives that align with your values. Emphasize the potential benefits of alternative approaches that prioritize patient safety and meet organizational goals.

6. Offer solutions: Rather than just raising concerns, consider proposing constructive solutions that address the ethical dilemma while still meeting organizational objectives. Present evidence-based methodologies or practices that offer a win-win scenario and maintain ethical standards.

7. Document interactions: Keep a record of your conversations, including dates, times, and individuals involved. This documentation serves as evidence of your commitment to resolving ethical conflicts and can be useful if further action needs to be taken.

Remember, advocating for ethical practices can be challenging, but it is crucial for the well-being of patients and your professional satisfaction. By following these steps, you can navigate ethical dilemmas while staying true to your personal and professional values.

Hi, I've always been an anxious person, but lately, it's becoming unmanageable. One example of a recent anxiety-inducing event was giving a presentation at work. It's great that you're seeking counseling to find coping techniques for your anxiety. It can be challenging to manage anxiety, but there are strategies that can help. One effective technique is deep breathing exercises. When you feel anxious, take slow and deep breaths in through your nose, holding it for a few seconds, then exhaling slowly through your mouth. This can help calm your nervous system and reduce the physical symptoms of anxiety.

Another helpful technique is called grounding. In moments of anxiety, focus on your environment and use your senses to bring yourself back to the present moment. Notice the texture of objects around you or listen carefully to the sounds in your surroundings. Engaging your senses can distract you from anxious thoughts and bring you into the present.

Additionally, practicing self-care is essential for managing anxiety. Make sure to prioritize activities that bring you joy and relaxation, such as engaging in hobbies, spending time in nature, practicing mindfulness or meditation, or even taking breaks throughout the day to do something you enjoy. Taking care of your physical health by getting regular exercise, eating nutritious meals, and getting enough sleep can also contribute to reducing anxiety levels.

Lastly, consider discussing your concerns with someone you trust, such as a close friend or family member. Sometimes sharing your feelings and experiences with others can provide relief and support. Don't hesitate to reach out to loved ones when you need them.

Remember, everyone's experience with anxiety is unique, so it may take some trial and error to find what works best for you. Be patient with yourself and give these techniques a try. If you find that your anxiety remains unmanageable despite implementing these strategies, I encourage you to seek professional assistance from a qualified mental health expert who can provide personalized guidance and support.

I was the one who ended it, and I'm so glad I did. It was the best decision I made in my life. But how do I stop the nightmares and flashbacks? It is creating a wall in my current relationship.

Ending an abusive relationship is often very difficult, especially if you were very close initially without the presence of abuse.  If the abuse included verbal or psychological condemnation, you will often have a negative self-image that you may "know" is not true but often feels very true. This negative self-image and fear of being abused again can activate protections in you that were needed at the time you were abused but now create a "wall" in your current relationship.  The fact that you were able to end the relationship and know that you made the right decision is a great acknowledgement that you have solid internal resources to draw upon in healing from the abuse.  Good for you!Nightmares and flashbacks are a strong sign of memories, including associated beliefs, emotions, and physical sensations, that have remained unprocessed and therefore unhealed.  There are likely reminders (called triggers) of the past abuse that are being activated in your current relationship that are allowing these unhealed memories to come to the surface and affect both your sleep and your waking experiences.  This is certainly not something you are purposefully doing but is the result of what happened to you.  However, you likely feel as if you are not in control.    The goal is protect your current relationship, evaluate your self-image for flaws in beliefs and feelings, and begin working on healing your memories of abuse. In many cases, my use of EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) would be helpful in reducing the emotional strength of your abuse memories, reduce or eliminate triggers, bring healing, and allow you to enjoy being in the present with your current relationship.  I would recommend discussing with your current partner your harmful past experiences, your decision to pursue counseling, and your strong desire to be healthy for your current relationship.  With a good support network in place, healing is very possible.

Managing anxiety can be a challenging journey, but there are indeed therapeutic approaches that can help you reduce its overwhelming grip on your life. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and mindfulness exercises have proven to be beneficial for many individuals struggling with anxiety.

In cognitive-behavioral therapy, the focus is on identifying and changing negative thought patterns that contribute to anxiety. This approach helps you challenge irrational thoughts and beliefs, enabling you to develop healthier ways of thinking. By working with a therapist trained in CBT, you can learn strategies to reframe anxious thoughts and gain a sense of control over them. These techniques can empower you to confront situations that trigger anxiety and gradually overcome them.

Mindfulness exercises, on the other hand, promote a deeper awareness of the present moment without judgment or attachment. Mindfulness can help you cultivate a calm and grounded state of mind, making it easier to navigate through anxious moments. Techniques like deep breathing, meditation, or body scans allow you to connect with your sensations and observe your thoughts and emotions more objectively. Practicing mindfulness regularly can help alleviate anxiety symptoms by bringing your attention back to the present instead of getting caught up in fearful anticipations.

Apart from these specific approaches, building a self-care routine into your daily life can also make a significant difference in managing anxiety. Taking care of yourself physically, emotionally, and mentally can create a solid foundation for resilience. Regular exercise, a balanced diet, sufficient sleep, and engaging in activities you enjoy can all support your overall well-being and enhance your ability to cope with anxiety.

It might be helpful to keep in mind that progress takes time and patience. As you engage in therapy or practice mindfulness exercises, remember to be compassionate with yourself during this process. It's essential not to get discouraged if setbacks occur, as they are natural parts of growth. Surrounding yourself with supportive friends and family who understand and validate your experiences can provide additional comfort and motivation.

Remember, this guidance is not meant as a substitute for professional therapy or medical advice. Reaching out to a mental health expert can provide you with personalized techniques and strategies tailored to your specific needs. How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?

Goodbyes can be hard.
Chances are most of the goodbyes you have experienced in your life have been
difficult. Saying goodbye to a therapist can be different. It can be an
opportunity to create a healthy ending in a positive relationship in your life.
If you work with a therapist who is skilled, then saying goodbye can be just as
transformative as the therapy itself. Ending therapy is also known
as “termination.” I know, “termination” doesn’t have a great ring to it!
However, it is what it is. It is an ending of the relationship as it existed.
It is reality cold and stark. Of course, when I talk to clients I don’t use the
word “termination,” I usually say “our goodbye.”  Under what circumstances does therapy usually
end? Therapy should end when a client does not need further assistance, is not
receiving any benefit from therapy, or might be harmed by continuing to work
with a particular therapist.In the best case scenario
the decision to move on from therapy and “say our goodbyes” happens when both
the therapist and the client feel like the client is ready to move on and move
up!  Ending the therapeutic relationship
should actually be worked on from the very first session. What I mean by that
is, there should be an understanding that the work we do together will have an
ending and that is a good thing because it means the client has gained the
skills to continue working on themselves independently. So the first session I
have with clients usually outlines a plan where the end goal is discussed and
we both have an understanding of the skills the client wants to learn or what
they hope to achieve. Now sometimes there are
situations where the therapist ends the relationship and the client may take
that personally, it is hard when any relationship ends and it might bring up
feelings of sadness, and fear or abandonment. Any good therapist will end the
relationship based on what is right for the client. What are some situations
where a therapist might end the relationship?If the situation the client
is dealing with is out of the therapist's scope of practice, the therapist may
end the relationship and refer the client to someone else. This is in the
client’s best interest. Another reason a therapist might end the relationship
is that the therapist is in a place in her life which prevents her from being
objective and helpful.  A therapist who
is going through a painful divorce may have difficulty working with a couple
that considering divorce. A good therapist may see that their judgement may be
clouded and want to refer the client to see someone else. This is good practice
and helps the client.If a client is actively
suicidal or actively using substances then the therapist may end the
relationship and refer out for a higher level of care. The client may need to
be hospitalized or may need an inpatient substance abuse treatment program.
Therapy may be terminated while they are being treated and may continue after
the intensive program is completed. 
Ending therapy should be a
time for connection and bringing together accomplishments, or reviewing the
next important step the client needs to take. It should not be an experience of
abandonment. A skilled therapist will help a client gain a new perspective on
closure. For some clients, it may be the one time in their lives when they get
a clean ending in a healthy relationship and they get to feel a sense of
control on creating that ending. Good luck to you!
