Doctor, I struggle with forming and maintaining social relationships. Whenever I'm in a group setting or even meeting new people one-on-one, I feel incredibly anxious and awkward. It makes me avoid social situations altogether, which leaves me feeling lonely and isolated. I am hoping to learn strategies to overcome my social anxiety and develop meaningful connections with others.

Building social relationships can indeed be challenging, especially when feelings of anxiety and awkwardness come into play. However, there are several strategies that you can try to help overcome your social anxiety and foster meaningful connections with others.

1. Start small: Begin by gradually exposing yourself to social situations rather than avoiding them altogether. You could start by attending smaller gatherings or meeting new people in low-pressure settings, such as joining a club or group that aligns with your interests.

2. Practice active listening: When engaging in conversations, focus on being present and attentive to the person you're talking to. Show genuine interest in what they have to say and ask open-ended questions that encourage further discussion. This not only helps build rapport but also takes some of the pressure off you to carry the conversation.

3. Challenge negative thoughts: Negative self-talk often contributes to feelings of anxiety and awkwardness. Take note of any negative thoughts that arise during social interactions and challenge them by asking yourself if there is evidence supporting these thoughts or if they are simply assumptions. Remind yourself of your positive qualities and past successes in social situations.

4. Seek support: Consider reaching out to trusted friends or family members who can provide encouragement and assistance. Sometimes having someone accompany you to social events can make it feel less intimidating. Having a support network can also give you the confidence to step outside your comfort zone and meet new people.

5. Join a support group: Connecting with others who may share similar experiences can be incredibly beneficial. Look for local support groups or online communities where you can discuss social anxiety, learn from others, and receive support from individuals who understand what you're going through.

6. Patience and self-compassion: Remember that building strong social relationships takes time and practice. Be patient with yourself and acknowledge that setbacks and moments of discomfort are normal parts of the process. Treat yourself with kindness and celebrate each small milestone along the way.

By applying these strategies consistently and gradually pushing yourself outside your comfort zone, you can make significant progress in overcoming social anxiety and creating meaningful connections with others. Remember, change takes time, so be patient and compassionate with yourself throughout this journey.

I'm feeling different towards my husband. I feel I am growing from the relationship. I have been with my husband for six years and married for almost five. I just don't feel that connection anymore. I feel nothing. I don't know why or if I'm just being irrational.

Lacey, I'm SO glad you wrote. Thousands of people are having this same feeling right now. I'm glad you're paying attention to it. When you first meet someone, there are all kinds of sparkly feelings and you both do and say lots of things to cement the attachment and create deep intimacy and connection. Then what happens is because we have that connection established, we instinctively cut back on those loving behaviours because we don't have to work hard to earn their love anymore. That sparkly feeling typically lasts a few years (long enough to procreate and keep the human race going), and then it wears off a bit, and you end up looking at each other thinking "how come I don't feel the same anymore?"Mostly (not always, and I'll get to that in a minute) all that this means is you've stopped doing all those loving things you used to do! It's as though you filled the car with gas, you've run out of gas now, and you're forgetting to put more in!The first clear solution to this feeling is to bring back more of your own loving behaviours that you've cut back on. Act lovingly, and you will likely regain those feelings. Talk to your partner about this. It's okay to say "do you remember we used to do X,Y and Z? Can we do that again? Can I get more of the foot rubs you used to give me?" Ask for what you want (instead of complaining). What are your 'love languages'? What are your partner's? Marriages need to be fed. It's that simple. Many things get in the way...children, jobs, but mostly complacency. Get active with your love!Okay, now, you might read this and think "that's not what's happening". My dad cheated on my mom for 13 years. I cannot stop obsessing over the fact that my boyfriend might be cheating on me even when I know he isn't. I have full access to his phone, social media, and e-mails. I never find anything, but I'm obsessed with constantly checking just in case. How do I stop this? It's driving a wedge between us.

Hi Greenville, I respect that you're owning your own overreactions, and that you want to give your boyfriend the respect he deserves. The truth is that some people cheat, and some don't, and our partners deserve the benefit of the doubt unless they show signs they can't be trusted.The answer here is in two different areas. Basically, if you want to feel differently (more trusting, in your case), you look at your thoughts, and your behaviours.Your thoughts are stuck... like tires in deep ruts in the road. These thoughts are only habits, they don't reflect the truth. Fear is probably whispering in your ear things like "everyone cheats", or " you're not enough for him". Once you figure out what fear is trying to tell you, picture those words in red next time they come up. Ask yourself what the evidence is that supports that thought (there won't be much...perhaps none), and what is the evidence that doesn't support it (I know lots of good men, I know I deserve love and loyalty, there is no sign of infidelity...). You're learning to refute the thoughts that are connected to the fear. That's the first half. Practise these thoughts.The rest of the work is in your behaviours. Act as though you trust him. Force yourself to not check or interrogate, and the less you check, the less obsessive and untrusting you will feel. Acting "as if" something if true strangely helps us believe it.It's possible to change the way we think, and this is turn changes the way we feel. Try this to start, and see a therapist for support and cognitive behavioural therapy if you want to dive more deeply into why this is happening and how to stop it. Good luck!

How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

Finding the right therapist is a lot like looking for a primary care doctor or family physician. You may have more than one in your life and also, if it does not work out, you can find a provider that is a better fit. You want to find someone who you believe will respond to your needs and help you accomplish your goals. That being said, it is very helpful to know what are you trying to accomplish in counseling. Therapists will open up the floor for you to discuss and will set treatment goals with you to move towards what you are accomplishing. This becomes the road map. The map keeps both the clinician and client on course. In addition, being very honest about your needs and providing feedback about sessions can be helpful. If you did not like something, make sure to speak up about it, so that it does not negatively impact the therapy relationship. If something works, make sure you speak up about that too. This can help the therapist to know if therapeutic changes need to be made. Similar to a doctor, if a medication is not working, it would be important to let them know so that adjustments can be made.  Therapy is a journey that is unique to each person. Talking about the therapy relationship is a part of that journey.

It's unfortunate to hear that you're experiencing such intense anxiety and panic attacks. It can be incredibly challenging when these feelings hinder your ability to leave the house or engage in everyday activities. Understanding the root causes of your anxiety and finding effective coping mechanisms are indeed crucial steps towards managing and addressing this.

To start, it may be helpful for you to explore potential triggers or patterns in your life that precede these episodes of anxiety and panic attacks. Reflecting on specific situations or circumstances that tend to induce stress can provide insights into what might be contributing to your symptoms. Writing down your experiences and emotions during these moments could help you identify common themes or possible triggers.

Once you have a better grasp of the potential contributors, consider incorporating relaxation techniques into your daily routine. Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, and mindfulness meditation are proven strategies to reduce anxiety levels. Experiment with different techniques to find one that resonates with you and practice it regularly, even outside of stressful situations. Being consistent will increase the chances of these techniques being effective when you need them most.

Seeking support from loved ones can also make a significant difference in managing anxiety. Opening up about what you've been going through and explaining how they can best support you can enable them to provide understanding and assistance when needed. Additionally, having someone to talk to during moments of distress can help calm your nerves and offer comfort.

Lastly, if you haven't already, consider making lifestyle changes that prioritize self-care and well-being. Engaging in regular exercise, maintaining a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and reducing caffeine consumption are all factors that can positively influence mental health. Taking time for yourself and engaging in activities you enjoy, whether that's reading, practicing hobbies, or spending time in nature, can further alleviate stress and promote a sense of calm.

Remember, it's essential to approach this journey of understanding and healing with patience and compassion for yourself. Progress takes time, and setbacks may happen, but with determination and a dedicated effort to self-care, you can learn to manage your anxiety and regain control of your everyday life.

Anxiety has been taking control of my life recently. I often experience rapid heartbeat, difficulty breathing, and intense fear in various situations. It affects my ability to socialize and even leaves me feeling physically unwell. I'm hoping that therapy can help me manage these anxious feelings so I can live a more fulfilling life.

Managing anxiety can be challenging, but there are several strategies that may help you regain control over your life. Here are some guidance and suggestions:

1. Deep breathing exercises: When you feel your anxiety escalating, focus on taking slow, deep breaths. Inhale deeply through your nose, hold for a few seconds, and then exhale slowly through your mouth. This technique can help regulate your heartbeat and reduce feelings of panic.

2. Progressive muscle relaxation: Tense each muscle group in your body one at a time, and then release the tension gradually. Starting from your toes, work your way up to your head. This method can promote physical relaxation and alleviate tension associated with anxiety.

3. Challenge negative thoughts: Anxiety often stems from irrational or distorted thinking patterns. Whenever you catch yourself having anxious thoughts, try to challenge them by asking yourself if there is any evidence supporting these thoughts. Look for alternative explanations and consider more realistic perspectives.

4. Create a soothing routine: Establishing a daily self-care routine can provide structure and stability amidst anxiety. Incorporate activities like exercise, proper nutrition, sufficient sleep, and relaxation techniques to support your overall well-being.

5. Gradual exposure: To overcome specific anxieties, such as socializing or facing certain situations, consider gradually exposing yourself to them in manageable steps. Start small, set achievable goals, and celebrate each milestone along the way. Over time, this approach can desensitize you to triggering situations.

6. Seek support: Talk to someone you trust about your anxiety, whether it's a supportive friend or family member. Sometimes, sharing your feelings can lessen their intensity. Additionally, consider joining a support group where you can connect with others who may have similar experiences.

7. Maintain a journal: Keeping a journal allows you to reflect on your thoughts and emotions, helping you gain insight into your triggers and patterns. It can also serve as a tool to track your progress and identify effective coping strategies.

8. Look after your overall well-being: Engage in activities that bring you joy, such as hobbies or creative outlets. Find ways to incorporate relaxation techniques into your daily routine, such as practicing mindfulness or engaging in calming activities like reading or listening to music.

Remember, managing anxiety is a journey, and what works for one person may not work for another. It's essential to be patient with yourself and celebrate small victories along the way. If possible, consider seeking professional help, where a therapist can provide individualized guidance tailored to your specific needs.

Developing a more positive view of yourself is a worthy goal, and therapy can definitely help you address deep-seated insecurities and challenge negative self-perceptions. While everyone's therapeutic journey is unique, there are some techniques and strategies that may be helpful for improving self-esteem.

One approach that therapists often use is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). This type of therapy focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns and beliefs that contribute to low self-esteem. In CBT, you would work collaboratively with a therapist to identify the specific thoughts and beliefs that fuel your negative self-perception. The environment at my workplace is toxic, filled with constant conflicts and power struggles. This is creating immense stress and tension, which ultimately impacts my well-being and job satisfaction. I hope counseling can provide guidance on how to navigate these workplace relationships effectively and maintain my mental health.

Navigating a toxic work environment can be incredibly challenging and it's understandable that you're feeling stressed and unsatisfied with your job. While counseling can provide support, there are also steps you can take to help improve the situation on your own.

1. Self-care: Prioritize taking care of yourself outside of work. Engage in activities that bring you joy and relaxation, such as exercise, hobbies, or spending time with loved ones. Taking care of your physical and mental well-being will give you resilience when dealing with workplace challenges.

2. Set boundaries: Clearly define your boundaries and communicate them assertively but respectfully with your colleagues. This can help protect your mental health by preventing others from overstepping personal limits and contributing to conflicts.

3. Seek support: Connect with colleagues who share similar experiences. Sharing your concerns and feelings with trusted coworkers can create a sense of solidarity and provide practical advice for managing difficult relationships at work.

4. Identify triggers: Reflect on specific situations or individuals that consistently lead to conflict or stress. By understanding what triggers these negative feelings, you can develop strategies to manage or even avoid those triggers altogether.

5. Communication skills: Develop effective communication skills to navigate workplace conflicts. Active listening, empathy, and clear expression of your needs or concerns can help foster healthier relationships and defuse tense situations.

6. Focus on what you can control: It's important to acknowledge that you may not have control over all aspects of your workplace environment. Instead, try to shift your focus towards what you do have control over, like how you respond to difficult situations and the actions you take to prioritize your own well-being.

7. Look for new opportunities: If the toxicity persists despite your efforts, consider exploring other job opportunities that align better with your values and goals. Keeping an eye out for potential roles within your organization or researching alternative career paths could assist in finding a more positive and fulfilling work environment.

Remember, each workplace is unique and the strategies that work for some may not work for others. It might take time and trial-and-error to find what works best for you in navigating these relationships effectively and maintaining your mental health. Patience with yourself during this process is essential.

Thank you for reaching out and sharing your struggles with self-harming behaviors. It takes courage to acknowledge the need for healthier coping mechanisms, and I want to support you in finding alternative ways to deal with your pain.

Understanding why individuals engage in self-harm can be complex and unique to each person, but it sounds like your experiences of enduring bullying and ongoing relationship difficulties might contribute to your self-harming behaviors. Firstly, I would encourage you to consider seeking professional help from a therapist or counselor who specializes in working with self-harm. They will provide you with personalized guidance and support throughout your healing journey.

In the meantime, there are some techniques and strategies you can try to manage self-harm urges. One approach is called distraction, which aims to redirect your attention away from self-harm towards more positive and healthy alternatives. Engaging in activities that occupy your mind, such as reading, drawing, writing, or playing a musical instrument, can often divert your focus from harmful thoughts and actions.

Another technique that may help is employing coping skills aimed at managing overwhelming emotions. Mindfulness exercises, deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, and guided imagery are all strategies that can aid in grounding yourself in the present moment, regulating your emotions, and decreasing distress.

Self-care practices are also essential when dealing with self-harm urges. Prioritizing activities that promote physical and emotional well-being can be crucial for maintaining stability. Remember that finding alternative coping strategies takes time and effort. Be patient and compassionate with yourself throughout this process. Consider seeking professional help to guide you further in understanding and addressing the underlying causes of self-harm.
